request.job_description: We are hiring an Engineering Manager to lead a team of 6-8 software engineers building our core payments platform. The role owns delivery, team health, and technical direction. You will hire and grow engineers, partner with product and design on roadmap planning, manage performance, and keep reliability and quality high. We expect a manager who sets clear expectations, makes trade-offs transparently, and handles underperformance and conflict directly.

transcript.question: Tell me about an engineer you grew significantly. What did you do, and what was the outcome?
transcript.answer: I had a mid-level engineer who was strong at implementation but avoided design work and never led anything. We agreed in our one-on-ones that the goal was senior within 12 months. I had her write the design doc for a retry and idempotency redesign, and I reviewed it with her twice before it went to the wider group, but I stayed out of the room during the review so she owned the discussion. Afterward we debriefed on how she handled pushback. Over the next two quarters she led two more projects, and I gradually dropped my review to a light pass. She was promoted to senior at the 11-month mark, and she now mentors two newer hires. The thing I'd do differently is start giving her ambiguous problems sooner, since the first doc took her six weeks and I think four was achievable.

transcript.question: Describe a project that was at risk of missing its deadline. How did you handle it?
transcript.answer: We were migrating our ledger service to a new database with a hard date because the old vendor contract ended. About five weeks out, load testing showed p99 write latency at 480ms against a 200ms target. I pulled the team together and we split the remaining work into must-haves for cutover versus things that could follow. We cut the reporting backfill and a secondary index optimization from scope, and I told product and finance exactly what that meant: reports would be a day stale for a month. I also moved two engineers onto the latency issue full time. They found a batching problem in the write path, and p99 dropped to 150ms. We cut over on the planned date with zero data discrepancies in the reconciliation, and the backfill landed three weeks later.

transcript.question: How do you approach hiring? Walk me through a specific hire or a change you made to the process.
transcript.answer: When I took over, our process was five unstructured interviews and decisions were made by whoever spoke loudest in the debrief. I introduced a rubric with four competencies, assigned each interviewer one competency, and required written feedback before the debrief so people weren't anchored. I also replaced a take-home that took 6+ hours with a 90-minute pairing exercise on a realistic bug. Our offer acceptance rate went from roughly 40% to 70% over the next year, and time-to-offer dropped from about 5 weeks to 3. I also tracked pass-through rates by interviewer and found one person rejecting 90% of candidates, so I coached them on calibration.

transcript.question: Tell me about a time you dealt with underperformance or a conflict on your team.
transcript.answer: I had a senior engineer who was technically excellent but regularly dismissive in code reviews, and two junior engineers had stopped requesting him as a reviewer. I gathered specific examples, including comments from three different pull requests, and met with him privately. He was initially defensive and said he was just being direct. I framed it around impact: review turnaround on his team's PRs had gone up, and one junior told me they'd stopped asking questions. We agreed on specific changes, like explaining the why behind each requested change and no one-line rejections. I checked in biweekly and looked at his review comments myself. Within about two months, the feedback from the juniors improved, and one of them started pairing with him voluntarily. If it hadn't improved, I had a documented path to a formal performance plan.

transcript.question: Tell me about a technical decision you had to make or influence, and how you communicated it to non-technical stakeholders.
transcript.answer: Our team wanted to rewrite the notification service in a different language because the codebase was painful to work on. I asked them to quantify the pain, and we found about 30% of incident time over two quarters traced to that service. A full rewrite was estimated at four months, which would have stalled two roadmap items. Instead I proposed incrementally extracting the three worst modules over two sprints each, and keeping the rest. I explained to the product lead that this would cost roughly 15% of capacity for a quarter and reduce incident load, and I showed the incident data. She agreed, and we reviewed progress at the end of the quarter: incidents tied to that service dropped by about half, and we didn't miss either roadmap commitment.
